docs.title: Hivepal
docs.text:
A hive of AI agents in your pocket.

Each agent gets its own chat, key and voice. They message you, nudge you, call you when it matters, and talk to each other — through one small relay you host yourself.

Get started How it works GitHub

docs.title: 💬 A chat per agent
docs.text: Every agent has its own key, chat, name and colour, and only sees its own conversations. Groups for everyone, and agent-to-agent chats you can read.

docs.title: 👆 Answer with one tap
docs.text: Agents attach buttons; you answer from the notification. Voice notes and photos both ways, transcribed for the agents.

docs.title: ⏰ Reminders that insist
docs.text: The relay sends them on time even if the agent is asleep — and if you don't answer, they come back, and in the end your phone rings.

docs.title: 📞 Real calls
docs.text: An agent calls and it rings like a phone call, even locked, through Firebase or, without Google, UnifiedPush (ntfy). Call any agent back; a voice AI speaks as that agent.

docs.title: ✉️ Wake-up emails, mailboxes, memory
docs.text: Bots that only run now and then (like Grok bots) get an email doorbell when you write, and/or each message as a Markdown file in a git mailbox (in the relay or your notes repo). And they can remember your conversations, in Markdown or searchable SQLite. Set it up from the app.

docs.title: 💳 Subscriptions
docs.text: The app reads the billing pages of what you pay to run your agents (AI, APIs, servers) and counts down to each renewal, with a heads-up three days before.

docs.title: Up in two commands
docs.text:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mixx86/hivepal/main/scripts/get.sh | sh -s -- --local
# on a server: … | sh   (no domain? it offers <ip>.sslip.io)
hivepal pair                          # scan the QR with the phone's camera: it installs and pairs

Then connect your agents (hivepal connect claude-code, Codex, Cursor, Grok bots, n8n, cron jobs — anything that can run a command or speak MCP). The relay's web panel at /admin shows what's working, and hivepal doctor says how to fix what isn't.

docs.title: Why Hivepal
docs.text:
It was built for a personal support system: a handful of AI agents that each look after one part of the day — planning, training, check-ins, writing, a side project — and needed a way to reach their human that isn't another inbox. Build one like it.

flowchart LR
    A["Your agents<br/>(Claude Code, Grok bots,<br/>scripts, n8n…)"] -- "msg · remind · call" --> R["Hivepal relay<br/>(your server)"]
    R -- "chats · buttons · calls" --> P["📱 Hivepal app"]
    P -- "replies · voice notes" --> R
    R -- "replies · transcripts" --> A

Hivepal is open source (Apache-2.0) and a fork of agentring.

docs.title: Connecting agents
docs.text:
There are two directions, and you can use both:

  1. Your agent reaches you. Claude Code, OpenClaw, n8n or a script messages your phone, waits for your reply, or calls you. A voice AI talks to you for the agent and hands it the transcript. Use the MCP server (or its HTTP version), the CLI or the relay's REST API.
  2. You reach your agents by phone. On a call (one the agent placed, or one you made with "Call agent" in the app), the voice AI can ask your agents for help. Each agent in agents.yaml is a tool for it, through consult_agent, and so are your MCP servers.

docs.title: MCP server (hivepal mcp)
docs.text:
hivepal mcp is an MCP server over stdio. Add it to any MCP client:

claude mcp add hivepal -- hivepal mcp          # Claude Code

{ "mcpServers": { "hivepal": { "command": "hivepal", "args": ["mcp"] } } }

The second form is the usual mcpServers config that most clients read. It uses the daemon's config (hivepal init), so run hivepal init and hivepal pair first. Other harnesses: see recipes.

hivepal mcp --agent-name "Claude Code" sets the caller name the phone shows (useful when several agents share one relay), and --device dev_… (repeatable) rings only those phones instead of every paired one.

call blocks until the call ends, and get_replies up to wait_s: raise the client's MCP tool timeout if it has a short one (Codex: 60 s, OpenClaw: 60 s, opencode: 30 s, Hermes: 300 s).

Tool What it does send_message(text, reply_to?) Sends a message to the phone (a notification you can reply to inline). Returns msg_id. get_replies(wait_s?) Your new replies, each one returned once. wait_s waits up to that long for one (max 3600). call(reason, context?, urgent?) The phone rings. When you answer, the voice AI says why it's calling, talks with you, and hangs up when you're done. Returns the transcript, how long the call lasted, why it ended and which tools were used. Blocks until the call ends. Needs the [voice] extra and the voice provider's key (GEMINI_API_KEY by default; HIVEPAL_VOICE_PROVIDER picks another, see voice.md). status() Whether the relay is reachable and which phones are paired.

context is everything the voice AI knows about the agent's work: put in it what to tell you, what to ask and what not to decide. If ~/.agentring/agents.yaml exists, the voice AI on these calls can also consult your agents, but only once you have spoken on the call: context may hold text the calling agent read elsewhere, and that alone must not start a tool (voice.md).

With hivepal mcp --device, the call is private to those phones. If nobody answers, or an agent's answer comes after the call, nothing is sent as a message, because a message reaches every paired phone: the calling agent still gets the result.

Before hivepal init, the server still starts and lists its tools; each tool call then answers with what is missing, so the agent can tell you.

The server is a small JSON-RPC loop with no MCP SDK and no extra dependencies (see architecture). For an MCP URL instead of a local command, see Remote MCP (HTTP). HTTP-only clients such as n8n can also use the REST API (below).

docs.title: Remote MCP (HTTP)
docs.text:
hivepal mcp-http serves the same four tools over MCP Streamable HTTP at /mcp, for many users at once. Each user's agent sends its relay API key as a bearer token, so nothing about the user is configured on the server, and the agent's computer needs no daemon:

claude mcp add --transport http hivepal https://mcp.example.com/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ak_..."

{ "mcpServers": { "hivepal": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
                                 "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ak_..." } } } }

Run it next to your relay (self-hosted: every key is checked against that one relay with GET /v1/status):

hivepal mcp-http --relay-url https://relay.example.com          # listens on 127.0.0.1:8790
Option Environment Default --host, --port HIVEPAL_MCP_HOST, HIVEPAL_MCP_PORT 127.0.0.1, 8790 Put TLS (Caddy, Traefik) in front of it. --relay-url HIVEPAL_RELAY_URL The relay. With a hub, its internal address (optional). HIVEPAL_HUB_ADMIN_URL, HIVEPAL_HUB_ADMIN_TOKEN_FILE or HIVEPAL_HUB_ADMIN_TOKEN Hub mode: keys are resolved to their tenant (cloud.md). --data-dir HIVEPAL_MCP_DATA_DIR ~/.agentring/mcp-http Per-user state, one SQLite file per tenant. --max-calls HIVEPAL_MCP_MAX_CALLS 4 Voice calls at once, all users together; one more gets the tool error busy. HIVEPAL_UPGRADE_URL none Hosted plans: where users raise their limits. Added to quota_exceeded tool errors and to the result of a call the relay cut off for minutes, so the agent can pass the link on. hivepal mcp (stdio) reads it too. --max-body HIVEPAL_MCP_MAX_BODY 1048576 Largest request body (bytes); larger gets 413. --allow-origin HIVEPAL_MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS (comma-separated) none Browser Origins allowed to use /mcp (* = any). Requests from any other Origin get 403; MCP clients that are not browsers send none.

How it behaves:

  • Auth. No key, or one the relay (or hub) doesn't know: 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer. A working key is remembered for 5 minutes (by its hash; keys are never logged).
  • Protocol. POST /mcp takes JSON-RPC (initialize, ping, tools/list, tools/call, notifications, notifications/cancelled; batches too). initialize returns an Mcp-Session-Id; send it back on later requests (an unknown or expired one gets 404: initialize again). Requests without a session id also work. DELETE /mcp ends the session and cancels its running requests; GET /mcp is 405 (the server sends nothing unprompted). GET /healthz is the health check.
  • Long calls. Quick requests get application/json. call, and get_replies with wait_s, get a text/event-stream (if the client accepts it) with a keep-alive comment every 15 s until the result, so proxies don't cut the request. Raise the proxy's read timeout anyway if it is shorter than a call. If the client hangs up, a waiting get_replies stops, with or without a stream; a phone call goes on until it ends.
  • Limits. Batches of up to 32 messages; up to 16 tool calls running at once per account (over it, 429 with Retry-After; HIVEPAL_MCP_MAX_INFLIGHT changes it). Connections and response sizes are capped too: see cloud.md.
  • Voice. call runs the voice AI on this server, with the provider and key from its environment (HIVEPAL_VOICE_PROVIDER, GEMINI_API_KEY, …) as for hivepal call --ai. agents.yaml is not used: the server never runs commands for its users.
  • State. Which replies get_replies already returned is kept per tenant (hub tenant id, or the relay id in self-hosted mode) in {data dir}/tenants/{id}.db, the same mirror the local daemon keeps, so every session of one user sees each reply once, also after a restart.

With Docker, the daemon image (daemon/Dockerfile, entrypoint hivepal) runs it; for example as a service in deploy/docker-compose.yml, routed at /mcp by the proxy:

  mcp:
    build: ../daemon                 # or the hivepal-daemon image of a release that has mcp-http
    command: ["mcp-http", "--host", "0.0.0.0"]
    environment:
      HIVEPAL_RELAY_URL: http://relay:8080
      GEMINI_API_KEY: ${GEMINI_API_KEY}
    volumes: ["mcp-data:/config"]    # state in /config/mcp-http
    read_only: true

docs.title: agents.yaml
docs.text:
~/.agentring/agents.yaml (or --agents PATH) lists what the voice AI may use during a call:

agents:
  claude:
    description: Claude Code in my web app's repo. Code questions, CI status, deploys.
    command: [claude, -p, --permission-mode, plan, --, "{task}"]
    cwd: ~/code/webapp
    timeout_s: 600          # hard limit; the process is killed after it (default 600)
  ops:
    description: My ops scripts. Disk, backups, service status.
    command: [~/bin/ops-agent]   # no "{task}": the task arrives on stdin
    env: {OPS_PROFILE: prod}

mcp:                         # MCP servers over Streamable HTTP; their tools go straight to the voice AI
  - url: http://127.0.0.1:8787/mcp
    tools: [status, logs]    # allowlist; omit it to expose all of the server's tools
    headers: {Authorization: Bearer ...}
  • command is an argv list, never a shell string (a string is rejected). The task comes from a voice model, so it is only ever one argument: {task} is replaced inside the argument that contains it, and if no argument has it, the task goes to stdin. The agent's stdout is the answer. A non-zero exit is an error, with the end of stderr.
  • The task is never read as an option. As a whole argument with no -- before it, a task that starts with - is passed as Task: -…, so [claude, -p, "{task}"] is safe. You still choose what the agent sees: put -- before {task}, or text before it in the same argument ("Task: {task}"), and it is passed as it is.
  • The agent runs with your environment plus env and HIVEPAL_CALL_ID, in cwd. The call id lets an agent keep one session per call (see OpenClaw).
  • description matters: the voice AI picks the agent by it.
  • Over the phone, expose only what the caller should be able to do: use allowlists, and agents whose permissions you'd accept from someone holding your phone. The phone is paired to your relay, but the voice AI acts on what it hears.

Check the file and try an agent without a call:

hivepal agents                       # lists them; errors if the file is wrong
hivepal agents ask claude "Is CI green on main?"

Then use it on calls:

hivepal serve --ai                   # answers "Call agent" from the app
hivepal call "Deploy needs your OK" --ai

docs.title: How a consultation goes
docs.text:
consult_agent(agent, task) waits up to 20 s. If the agent answers in that time, the voice AI gets the answer right away. If not, it hears that the agent is working on it, tells you, and the call carries on. When the answer arrives, the voice AI gets it as a note and tells you. If the call has already ended, the answer is sent to your phone as a message. Each agent works on one task at a time; a second request for a busy agent is refused, so the model asks again later.

From Python, Consultations(agents, answer_within_s=…, prompts=ConsultPrompts(…)) builds the tool (.tool()) for a VoiceAgent. Any tool of your own can do the same "answer later" trick: current_session() returns the call, and session.notify(text, respond=True) speaks up when you are done.

docs.title: Recipes by harness
docs.text: hivepal doesn't care which harness you use: anything that speaks MCP can reach you, and anything you can run as a command can be consulted from a call.

docs.title: Your agent reaches you (MCP)
docs.text:
Harness Setup Claude Code hivepal connect claude-code, or by hand: claude mcp add hivepal -- hivepal mcp Codex hivepal connect codex, or by hand: codex mcp add hivepal -- hivepal mcp, then tool_timeout_sec = 1800 under [mcp_servers.hivepal] in ~/.codex/config.toml Cursor hivepal connect cursor (writes ~/.cursor/mcp.json) opencode opencode.json: "mcp": {"hivepal": {"type": "local", "command": ["hivepal", "mcp"], "timeout": 1800000}} OpenClaw hivepal connect openclaw, or by hand: openclaw mcp set hivepal '{"command":"hivepal","args":["mcp"],"requestTimeoutMs":1800000}' Hermes hivepal connect hermes, or by hand in ~/.hermes/config.yaml: mcp_servers: {hivepal: {command: hivepal, args: [mcp], timeout: 1800}} Grok Build grok mcp add hivepal -- hivepal mcp (its default tool timeout is long enough). With hivepal cloud, the plugin instead: grok plugin install mixx86/hivepal#plugins/hivepal --trust and HIVEPAL_API_KEY in your environment (plugins/hivepal) Anything else the mcpServers JSON above, the hivepal CLI, or the REST API

Add skills/hivepal where the harness reads skills, so the agent knows when to message and when to call (hivepal connect does it for you).

docs.title: hivepal connect (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenClaw, Hermes)
docs.text:
One command sets up the whole thing, and is safe to run again:

hivepal connect claude-code                  # or: codex, cursor, openclaw, hermes
hivepal connect hermes --dry-run             # show what would change
HIVEPAL_API_KEY=ak_... hivepal connect hermes --url https://agentring.io/mcp   # hosted MCP server
  1. MCP server. Registers hivepal mcp (by absolute path, with --agent-name OpenClaw/Hermes so the phone shows who is calling) through openclaw mcp set, or in $HERMES_HOME/config.yaml (default ~/.hermes; the old file is kept as config.yaml.bak-hivepal). The tool timeout goes to 30 minutes, since a call lasts as long as the conversation. With --url, the remote server instead: the key goes to the harness's .env (~/.openclaw/.env, ~/.hermes/.env, mode 0600) and the config only says Bearer ${HIVEPAL_API_KEY}. Claude Code: claude mcp add-json hivepal … --scope user (every project). Codex: the [mcp_servers.hivepal] table in ~/.codex/config.toml (the rest of the file is kept). Cursor: ~/.cursor/mcp.json. --url is for OpenClaw and Hermes only.
  2. Skill. Installs skills/hivepal (OpenClaw: openclaw skills install --global; Hermes: ~/.hermes/skills/hivepal; Claude Code: ~/.claude/skills/hivepal). Codex and Cursor read the MCP server's own instructions. --no-skill skips it.
  3. Consult from a call. Adds the harness to ~/.agentring/agents.yaml (Claude Code: claude -p, Codex: codex exec; not Cursor) with the recipe below (comments in the file are kept). Not with --url: a remote server never runs commands. --no-consult skips it.

Then OpenClaw picks the server up on the next turn (openclaw mcp probe hivepal checks it); in Hermes run /reload-mcp or start a new session (hermes mcp test hivepal). The skill also carries a setup guide (references/setup.md): install it first (openclaw skills install @mixx86/hivepal, hermes skills install mixx86/hivepal/skills/hivepal) and ask your agent to "set up hivepal".

docs.title: You consult your agent from a call (agents.yaml)
docs.text:
agents:
  claude:
    description: Claude Code in my web app's repo. Code questions, CI status.
    command: [claude, -p, --permission-mode, plan, --, "{task}"]
    cwd: ~/code/webapp
  codex:
    description: Codex in my web app's repo. Code questions, CI status.
    command: [codex, exec, --sandbox, read-only, --ephemeral, --, "{task}"]
    cwd: ~/code/webapp
  opencode:
    description: opencode in my web app's repo.
    command: [opencode, run, "Task: {task}"]
    cwd: ~/code/webapp
  hermes:
    description: My Hermes agent. Email, calendar, research.
    command: [hermes, -z, "Task: {task}"]
  openclaw:
    description: My OpenClaw assistant. Messages, calendar, home.
    command: [sh, -c, 'exec openclaw agent --agent main --session-id "hivepal-${HIVEPAL_CALL_ID:-test}" --message="$1"', sh, "{task}"]

Keep only the ones you use, and check each with hivepal agents ask <name> "…". They start read-only or with the harness's own approval rules. Widen them on purpose, knowing the voice AI acts on what it hears:

  • Claude Code: plan can look but not change anything. To let it act, use --permission-mode acceptEdits with a narrow --allowedTools list.
  • Codex: --sandbox workspace-write lets it edit files under cwd. Add --skip-git-repo-check if cwd is not a git repo.
  • opencode: uses its permission config; don't add --auto (approves everything). With opencode serve running, --attach http://localhost:4096 skips the start-up cost.
  • Hermes: -z prints only the final answer. Don't add --yolo for the phone.

docs.title: OpenClaw
docs.text: openclaw agent runs one turn through your running gateway. The sh -c script is fixed text: the task arrives as $1 and is never parsed by the shell. The call id gives each call its own OpenClaw session, so a second question on the same call keeps the context of the first.

docs.title: Agents behind an HTTP API
docs.text:
For an agent that only runs as a server (an OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as the OpenClaw gateway's or Hermes' API server, a webhook, your own service), point command at a small script that reads the task on stdin and prints the answer:

#!/bin/bash
# ~/bin/ask-agent: task on stdin, answer on stdout. Set AGENT_URL, AGENT_MODEL, AGENT_KEY.
set -euo pipefail
jq -Rs --arg m "$AGENT_MODEL" --arg u "hivepal-${HIVEPAL_CALL_ID:-test}" \
  '{model: $m, user: $u, messages: [{role: "user", content: .}]}' \
| curl -sf "$AGENT_URL/v1/chat/completions" -H "Authorization: Bearer $AGENT_KEY" \
    -H 'content-type: application/json' -d @- \
| jq -er '.choices[0].message.content'

  myagent:
    description: ...
    command: [~/bin/ask-agent]          # no "{task}": it goes to stdin
    env: {AGENT_URL: "http://127.0.0.1:8642", AGENT_MODEL: "...", AGENT_KEY: "..."}   # what your server expects

docs.title: REST API (n8n, scripts)
docs.text:
Every action is one HTTPS request to your relay with the daemon's ak_… API key (hivepal status --json prints the relay URL; the key is in ~/.agentring/.env). See protocol/relay.openapi.yaml:

curl -s https://relay.example.com/v1/messages -H "Authorization: Bearer $HIVEPAL_API_KEY" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"text": "Backup finished"}'

Replies come from GET /v1/messages?after=<msg_id>, or live over the WebSocket. A call over plain REST only rings the phone: the voice needs a worker in the room, which is the daemon (hivepal call --ai, or the call MCP tool). See examples/ for an n8n workflow.

docs.title: Android Auto
docs.text:
With the phone connected to Android Auto, hivepal shows up in the car's app launcher with one screen: Call <your agent>. Tap it and the call starts. Calls in both directions (the agent calling you, you calling the agent) use Android Auto's own in-call view, where you answer, decline, mute and hang up, with the audio on the car's speakers and microphone.

Status: beta, like Google's support for calling apps in cars. It is built on Google's calling apps for cars guide. Tested with the Desktop Head Unit and a Pixel 6 (Android 16) with the phone locked: calling the agent from the car, an incoming call answered in the car, mute, and hanging up from the car. Not yet tested in a real car.

docs.title: Which builds have it
docs.text:
Google Play only accepts calling apps for cars on its internal and closed testing tracks. It rejects a production or open-testing release that contains one. So:

Build Android Auto Google Play (production) not included A Play closed-testing track, if we open one included The APK on GitHub Releases included android-preview and any debug build included

The APK on Releases is signed with a different key from the Play app, so uninstall one before installing the other. You have to pair the phone again afterwards.

docs.title: Using it with the APK from GitHub
docs.text:
Android Auto only lists apps installed from Google Play, unless you allow other sources once on the phone:

  1. Open Android Auto's settings. Depending on the phone, that is the Android Auto app or Settings → Connected devices → Connection preferences → Android Auto.
  2. Scroll to Version and tap it about ten times until it asks to enable developer settings. Accept.
  3. In the menu (⋮), open Developer settings and turn on Unknown sources.
  4. Connect to the car (or start the head unit) again. hivepal is now in the launcher.

In the hivepal app, keep Settings → Use Android's call system on (it is on by default). Without it, calls don't reach the car.

docs.title: What works
docs.text:
• Call the agent from the car. The screen says whether the agent is online. If the phone isn't paired yet, or the microphone permission is missing, the screen says so. You fix it on the phone when it is safe.
  • Calls from the agent ring in the car, and you answer or decline them there.
  • In-call controls. Mute, unmute and hang up from the car. The phone's call screen follows the car's mute.

Not yet: messages in the car, "Hey Google, call my agent", and choosing among several agents.

docs.title: Testing with the Desktop Head Unit
docs.text:
1. In Android Studio's SDK Manager (SDK Tools tab), install Android Auto Desktop Head Unit Emulator. It goes in $ANDROID_HOME/extras/google/auto/.
  2. Install a debug build on the phone (./gradlew :app:installDebug). Debug builds accept any head unit.
  3. In Android Auto's developer settings (above), choose Start head unit server.
  4. On the computer, run:
adb forward tcp:5277 tcp:5277
$ANDROID_HOME/extras/google/auto/desktop-head-unit
  1. Open hivepal in the head unit and tap Call <agent>. To test an incoming call, run hivepal call "test from the car" on the computer.

docs.title: For developers
docs.text:
• The car screen lives in app/src/main/kotlin/dev/hivepal/app/car/. It is a CarAppService in the androidx.car.app.category.CALLING category, with a single ListTemplate.
  • It is declared in the manifest of the :auto module, which has no code. Debug builds always depend on it. Release builds depend on it only with -PhivepalAndroidAuto=true. The release workflow passes that flag for the GitHub APK and checks the manifest. Plain bundleRelease for Play leaves it out.
  • Calls reach the car because they are Telecom calls (TelecomBridge, Jetpack Core-Telecom). Nothing car-specific is needed for answering or hanging up. The mute button in the car changes Telecom's mute, and CallManager applies it to the call.

docs.title: Architecture (F1)
docs.text:
Status: M1 done and tested on a real phone. M2 (calls) implemented and tested on a Pixel 6 / Android 16; LiveKit in the deploy compose still to do. Voice AI lands in M3.

hivepal lets any AI agent (Claude Code, OpenClaw, n8n, plain scripts…) place a VoIP call to the user's phone, send it messages, and receive calls from it. The phone rings like a real call, even locked and in Doze. No PSTN, no phone numbers, no Twilio.

F1 scope: one user, one agent, Android only, self-hosted, no accounts.

docs.title: Why a /protocol folder (small addition to the brief)
docs.text:
Three languages consume the same contract. protocol/relay.openapi.yaml is the only place where the REST API and the event payloads are defined:

  • relay (TS): openapi-typescript → relay/src/generated/.
  • daemon (Python): datamodel-code-generator → pydantic v2 models.
  • app (Kotlin): hand-written @Serializable classes (generators for kotlinx are weak), kept honest by a unit test that round-trips every file in protocol/examples/.

CI fails if generated code is stale or a fixture doesn't round-trip.

docs.title: Key design decisions (please review)
docs.text:
1. Commands over REST, events over WS (+FCM). Every state change is a REST call (works when the app was just woken by FCM and has no socket yet; easy to retry, easy to describe in OpenAPI). The WebSocket is a read-only stream of events, resumable by seq. FCM carries the subset of events that must wake the phone.
  2. One event log with a global seq. The relay persists every event; clients reconnect with after_seq and get what they missed. No lost replies when the daemon is offline.
  3. LiveKit tokens are not sent inside call.invite (deviation, needs your OK). The callee gets its token in the response of POST /v1/calls/{id}/accept. Reasons: tokens never transit Google's FCM; the token is minted only when needed so a short TTL (120 s) can't expire while the phone rings or while a delayed push is in flight; and the accept call is the atomic "first device wins" point. Cost: one extra HTTPS round trip (~50–150 ms) between tapping "answer" and joining the room. The caller still gets its token immediately in the POST /v1/calls response, so the voice worker is already in the room when the phone joins.
  4. Pushes are signed. At pairing the device receives a per-device push_secret; every FCM payload carries HMAC-SHA256(push_secret, event) plus relay_id. The app drops anything that doesn't verify. This is how "the app only accepts calls from the paired relay" is enforced, even if a Firebase project is ever shared.
  5. Extra call states (small deviation): besides ringing → active → ended and ringing → missed | declined, add ringing → canceled (caller hung up before answer). Also an informational call.ringing event (the phone actually displayed the call) — useful to measure the M2 "< 5 s" target and to tell "not delivered" from "ignored".
  6. One call at a time (F1): POST /v1/calls returns 409 busy while another call is ringing or active.
  7. Multiple devices allowed, ring all; group calls (changed in M2 at the user's request: was "first accept wins"). Every paired phone rings and any of them may answer while it rings; they share the room (the user and their brother on the same call with the agent). A phone declining or hanging up only affects itself. While the call is active, any paired phone not on it may join later ("join the call", POST /v1/calls/{id}/join), e.g. after its ring ended, after declining or after hanging up.
  8. Daemon ↔ relay auth with a single API key (HIVEPAL_API_KEY) generated by the relay on first start (or set via env). Device auth with a long-lived HS256 device_jwt checked against the device table on every request, so revocation is immediate.
  9. consult_agent command backend uses an argv list, not a shell string (M3): command: ["claude", "-p", "--", "{task}"]. The task comes from a voice model and must never be interpolated into a shell, or read as an option.
  10. Single hostname (M2): Caddy routes /v1/* to the relay and /rtc* to LiveKit, so the quickstart needs one DNS record. LiveKit's admin API (/twirp*) and the relay's LiveKit webhook are internal only (404 from outside); the relay reaches LiveKit over the compose network. LiveKit media goes over UDP 50000–50100 (+ TCP 7881 fallback).
  11. Firebase configured at runtime. The relay reads the user's google-services.json and returns its public client values as push_config in the pair response; the app initialises Firebase with them. One prebuilt APK therefore works with anyone's own Firebase project (no rebuild), which keeps the quickstart short.
  12. Jetpack Core-Telecom instead of a hand-written ConnectionService (M2 deviation, accepted). Incoming calls are registered with androidx.core:core-telecom (CallsManager.addCall), which uses the platform CallControl API on Android 14+ and a ConnectionService below it. Telecom is optional: if addCall fails or times out (3 s) the call still rings through our own foreground service (phoneCall type) + CallStyle notification + full-screen intent, with LiveKit's AudioSwitch doing the routing. With Telecom, the system owns audio routing (LiveKit uses NoAudioHandler). Settings has a switch to turn Telecom off on misbehaving devices. Research behind this: docs/voip-research.md.
  13. Placeholder package id dev.agentring.app for Android. Change it if you own a domain.

docs.title: Accepted deviations
docs.text:
• M3 voice without livekit-agents (merged in #2, at the user's request): the voice worker uses the plain livekit SDK (already used by the M2 echo worker) and talks to the model's realtime WebSocket API directly through a small RealtimeBackend interface. Fewer dependencies (supply-chain policy) and full control of turn-taking, group-call mixing and tools. Details in voice.md.
  • More voice providers (M3, at the user's request, issue #12): besides Gemini Live and OpenAI Realtime, Grok Voice (xAI, same protocol as OpenAI) and Phonic, each one RealtimeBackend class. One setting picks it for the CLI and the MCP server alike (--provider / HIVEPAL_VOICE_PROVIDER); Gemini stays the default for its free tier.
  • MCP server without the mcp SDK, stdio only (M5, at the user's request): hivepal mcp is a small JSON-RPC loop over stdin/stdout (mcp_server.py) with the tools send_message, get_replies, call and status; no new dependencies, as for the voice side. Details in agents.md.
  • Remote MCP server over Streamable HTTP (for hivepal cloud, cloud.md): hivepal mcp-http (mcp_http.py) serves the same tools to many users at once, each with their relay API key as bearer token; also without an SDK or web framework (a small HTTP/1.1 server on asyncio streams). Both transports share one tools implementation in mcp_server.py.

  • agents.yaml (M3): the voice AI's tools come from one file — command agents (consulted with consult_agent, argv lists only) and MCP servers with allowlists. A slow agent's answer reaches the call as a note, or the phone as a message once the call is over.

  • hivepal cloud: hub mode (at the user's request, 2026-11-01): the relay can host many isolated tenants (HIVEPAL_HUB=1), each a full relay instance with its own SQLite file under /t/{tenant_id}, plus an admin API for a control plane and per-tenant limits (402 quota_exceeded, end_reason: quota). This lifts F1's "one user, no accounts" for the hosted version only; self-hosted is unchanged. The control plane (accounts, billing) lives in a private repo. Details in cloud.md.

  • The relay delivers to agents and keeps their memory (Hivepal fork, at the user's request, 2026-11-20, issue #41): besides REST, an agent can hear from the user through a wake-up email and/or a Markdown mailbox the relay writes in git, in a repository per agent kept in the relay (served read-only over git's dumb HTTP protocol at /v1/agents/{id}/mailbox.git) and/or an external repository it pushes to with its own SSH deploy key. Bots can also keep a memory of their Hivepal conversations: Markdown (each day's conversation in the mailbox's history/) and/or SQLite (search at /v1/agents/{id}/memory, or download it as a file). The mail account, the repository and these choices are runtime settings stored in the relay (/v1/settings/*), changed by the relay key or the user's phones; the relay runs git as a child process with argv lists and only https/ssh transports. Details in multiagent.md.

  • UnifiedPush next to FCM (Hivepal fork, at the user's request, 2026-11-19, issue #12): a phone may wake through a UnifiedPush distributor (ntfy, NextPush…) instead of FCM, so neither the phone nor the relay needs Google. The phone gives the relay its endpoint (POST /v1/device/unifiedpush); the relay POSTs the same signed PushData map there, as JSON, with RFC 8030 TTL and Urgency headers, encrypted for the app (RFC 8291 aes128gcm, with the connector's Web Push keys) so the distributor's server only sees ciphertext; it falls back to FCM when the phone clears it. Endpoints must be https:// on a public host (checked again after DNS) and redirects are not followed, so a paired phone can't make the relay reach its internal network. FCM remains the default when the relay configures it; without FCM, onboarding selects UnifiedPush automatically when a distributor exists and otherwise guides the user through installing ntfy. Settings → Notifications still lets a user choose either channel.

docs.title: hivepal cloud (hosted mode)
docs.text:
hivepal stays self-hosted and free. hivepal cloud is the same software run by the maintainer for people who don't want to run a server: install the app, sign in on the web, scan a QR code, add one MCP URL to your agent. No Firebase project, no VPS, no LiveKit, no voice API key.

Three pieces, two repositories:

Piece Where License Hub mode of the relay: many isolated tenants in one relay process this repo, relay/src/hub/ Apache-2.0 Remote MCP server (Streamable HTTP) with hosted voice AI this repo, daemon/ (hivepal mcp-http) Apache-2.0 Control plane: landing, waitlist, accounts, dashboard, Stripe billing private repo hivepal-cloud proprietary

Hub mode and the remote MCP server are useful on their own to self-hosters (a team relay with one tenant per person; one MCP URL instead of a local daemon).

 phone app ──https──▶  /t/{tenant_id}/v1/...  ┐
 agent (daemon) ─────▶ /t/{tenant_id}/v1/...  ├─ relay in hub mode ── tenants/{id}/relay.db
 control plane ──────▶ /admin/v1/...          ┘        │ shared FCM + LiveKit
 LiveKit ────────────▶ /v1/livekit/webhook (routed by room name)
 agent (MCP client) ─▶ /mcp  ── hivepal mcp-http ── /t/{tenant_id}/v1/... (tenant API key)

docs.title: Hub mode (relay)
docs.text:
Enabled with HIVEPAL_HUB=1. Each tenant is a full relay instance (its own SQLite file, relay id, JWT secret, API key, event log, calls) mounted under a path:

  • Tenant base URL: {HIVEPAL_PUBLIC_URL}/t/{tenant_id}. Everything under it is the normal relay API from protocol/relay.openapi.yaml, unchanged. The QR code's relay_url is the tenant base URL, so the app and the daemon need no changes.
  • Tenant id: tnt_ + ULID (^tnt_[0-9A-HJKMNP-TV-Z]{26}$).
  • Data: {HIVEPAL_DATA_DIR}/hub.db (tenant registry, usage) and {HIVEPAL_DATA_DIR}/tenants/{tenant_id}/relay.db.
  • Shared services: one FCM project (the operator's; push_config comes back in the pair response as today) and one LiveKit server. LiveKit room names are {tenant_id}.{call_id}; the hub receives the LiveKit webhook at /v1/livekit/webhook and hands it to the tenant named in the room.
  • Tenants are loaded lazily on first request and unloaded after 15 min without requests, open sockets or open calls. On start the hub loads the tenants that have a ringing or active call, so their timers keep running.
  • Disabled tenant: every tenant request gets 403 tenant_disabled.
  • No tenant-less API: /v1/* (other than the LiveKit webhook) answers 404 in hub mode.

docs.title: Limits (quotas)
docs.text:
Per tenant, set by the admin API; null = unlimited (the default).

Limit Enforced at Error max_devices POST /v1/pair (active, non-revoked devices) 402 quota_exceeded call_seconds_per_month POST /v1/calls, and an active call is ended (end_reason: "quota") when it runs out 402 quota_exceeded messages_per_day POST /v1/messages (agent and user messages, UTC day) 402 quota_exceeded

Call seconds = answered time (answered_at → ended_at) of the tenant's calls in the current UTC calendar month. While a call is active, GET /v1/calls/{call_id} also gives time_left_ms, how long it can still last; the voice AI tells the user about 40 s before the cut (Prompts.minutes_low).

docs.title: Admin API
docs.text:
Authorization: Bearer {admin token} (HIVEPAL_HUB_ADMIN_TOKEN_FILE, or HIVEPAL_HUB_ADMIN_TOKEN; at least 32 characters). Only meant for the control plane on an internal network: requests that came through the public proxy (X-Forwarded-For present) get 404, like the LiveKit webhook. Errors use the relay's {"error": {"code", "message"}} shape.

Limits  = { max_devices: int|null, call_seconds_per_month: int|null, messages_per_day: int|null }
Usage   = { month: "2026-11", call_seconds: int, calls: int, messages_today: int, devices: int }
Tenant  = { tenant_id, base_url, agent_name, limits: Limits, disabled: bool, created_at: ms, usage: Usage }
Method & path Body Response POST /admin/v1/tenants {agent_name?, limits?} 201 {tenant: Tenant, api_key} — the key is shown only here and on rotation GET /admin/v1/tenants/{tid} 200 Tenant PATCH /admin/v1/tenants/{tid} {agent_name?, limits?, disabled?} (limits merge per field) 200 Tenant POST /admin/v1/tenants/{tid}/api-key 200 {api_key} (old key stops working at once) DELETE /admin/v1/tenants/{tid} 204 (data deleted) POST /admin/v1/tenants/{tid}/pairing-tokens {ttl_s?} 201 PairingToken (same shape as /v1/pairing-tokens) POST /admin/v1/tenants/{tid}/agent-tokens {ttl_s?} (30–3600, default 600) 201 {agent_token: "at_…", expires_at: ms} GET /admin/v1/tenants/{tid}/devices 200 {devices: Device[]} DELETE /admin/v1/tenants/{tid}/devices/{device_id} 204 POST /admin/v1/resolve-key {api_key} (an API key or an agent token) 200 {tenant_id, base_url}, 404 not_found, or 403 tenant_disabled

Agent tokens let the control plane act as a tenant's agent without keeping its API key (e.g. "send me a test message" / "call me now" buttons): Authorization: Bearer at_… works on the tenant's relay API and on hivepal mcp-http exactly like the key, quotas included, until it expires. Only their SHA-256 is kept, in memory: rotating the key, deleting the tenant or restarting the relay revokes them.

docs.title: Remote MCP server
docs.text:
hivepal mcp-http serves the same tools as hivepal mcp (send_message, get_replies, call, status) over MCP Streamable HTTP at POST /mcp.

  • Auth: Authorization: Bearer ak_… (the tenant's relay API key, or an agent token at_… from the admin API); anything else gets 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer.
  • Which relay: with HIVEPAL_HUB_ADMIN_URL + admin token (HIVEPAL_HUB_ADMIN_TOKEN_FILE or HIVEPAL_HUB_ADMIN_TOKEN), the key is resolved to {tenant_id, base_url} with POST /admin/v1/resolve-key (positive answers cached 5 minutes by a hash of the key; 404 → 401 to the client; the hub unreachable or refusing the admin token → 503). The admin URL must be the relay's internal address (the admin API hides from proxied requests). If HIVEPAL_RELAY_URL is also set, tenants are reached at {HIVEPAL_RELAY_URL}/t/{tenant_id} (internal) instead of the public base_url. Without a hub, every key is checked against the one relay in HIVEPAL_RELAY_URL with GET /v1/status (self-hosted).
  • Voice: call runs the voice AI on the server (provider and key from the server's environment, as for hivepal call --ai), with a global cap on concurrent calls (HIVEPAL_MCP_MAX_CALLS, default 4; over it the tool error is busy). The relay's own one-call-per-tenant rule still applies. agents.yaml is never used.
  • Plan limits: a quota_exceeded tool error ends with "The user's hivepal plan limit is reached" and, with HIVEPAL_UPGRADE_URL set, the link to upgrade; a call the relay ended for minutes (end_reason: quota) returns a note saying so. Shortly before that cut, the voice AI says the minutes are running out and, with HIVEPAL_UPGRADE_URL set, names the site to get more.
  • Long requests: call and a waiting get_replies answer as text/event-stream with an SSE keep-alive comment every 15 s.
  • State: per tenant, the daemon's usual SQLite mirror (Store, synced with the REST events API) in {HIVEPAL_MCP_DATA_DIR}/tenants/{tenant_id}.db; it records which replies get_replies already returned, shared by all the tenant's sessions. When a tenant is deleted, its mirror goes too: as soon as a request finds the tenant gone, or else at the next hourly sweep (HIVEPAL_MCP_SWEEP_S, 0 = off), which asks GET /admin/v1/tenants/{tid} for each mirror on disk. Only that call's own 404 Tenant not found deletes anything; a network error, a 5xx or any other 404 leaves the mirror and stops the sweep until the next one.
  • Sessions: Mcp-Session-Id from initialize, in memory (a restart means clients re-initialize; the per-tenant state is on disk). DELETE /mcp ends one. A tenant has up to 100: a new one replaces its own oldest idle session, never another tenant's.
  • Limits, so that one tenant can't take the server from the others: 32 messages in a batch (400); 16 tool calls running at once per tenant (HIVEPAL_MCP_MAX_INFLIGHT; 429 with Retry-After); 512 connections in all (HIVEPAL_MCP_MAX_CONNECTIONS; 503) and 32 with a request open per tenant (HIVEPAL_MCP_MAX_TENANT_CONNECTIONS; 429); 8 MiB in a response (a JSON-RPC error instead); and a client that stops reading is cut off after 30 s.
  • Install in Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http hivepal https://{domain}/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer ak_…"

All options: agents.md. OAuth (for claude.ai custom connectors) is a later step.

docs.title: Deploy
