docs.title: FAQ and troubleshooting
docs.text: Something not working? Start with hivepal doctor (in Docker: docker compose exec daemon hivepal doctor): it checks the relay, its certificate, the key, push, calls, voice and the paired phones, and says what to do about each problem.

docs.title: Messages only arrive when the app is open
docs.text: If the relay has Firebase, configure it (Firebase), run the installer again and re-pair the phone. Without Firebase, setup automatically uses UnifiedPush: install its suggested distributor (such as ntfy) and return to the app. You can also choose UnifiedPush manually in Settings → Notifications. Status in the app says whether pushes work.

docs.title: A locked phone doesn't ring
docs.text:
1. In the app: Settings → Calls shows what's missing (notifications, full-screen calls, battery).
  2. The manufacturer's battery saver kills it: per brand.
  3. Test: Ring me in 10 s (at the end of the setup, or in Settings), then lock the phone; or hivepal call "test" with the screen off.

docs.title: "refusing plain http://"
docs.text: The CLI and the app only send keys over http:// to private addresses (LAN, Tailscale). For a public server use HTTPS (the server install does it with Caddy).

docs.title: An agent never answers
docs.text: Agents shows when it was last seen. Red after a day: its routine stopped. With wake-up emails, hivepal bots shows ✉ next to agents that have an address; check HIVEPAL_SMTP_URL and the relay's logs (docker compose logs relay | grep wake). An agent that reads a mailbox folder needs hivepal mailbox running from cron with its key: the files appear only when that runs (mailbox files).

docs.title: The relay restarts after an update or the server runs out of memory
docs.text: Build the images on your computer: scripts/deploy-images.sh user@server. See keeping a small server light.

docs.title: A subscription says "No date found"
docs.text: The page you picked doesn't show the date as text the app recognises. Tap Change page and pick the page that literally says when it renews (often Billing, Plan or Manage subscription). If it still fails, open an issue with the service's name and the sentence that shows the date.

docs.title: "Continue with Google" in Subscriptions
docs.text: It opens Google's account chooser in its own window, which closes once you continue. If Google says instead that the browser or app may not be secure (it does when it wants your Google password typed there), log in to that service with email and password or an email code.

docs.title: Which APK do I install?
docs.text:
Built from Signed with For hivepal-X.Y.Z.apk in a release a version tag the release key most people hivepal.apk in android-preview every change on main the public debug key trying what's next

scripts/build-app.sh builds like android-preview. Within a channel each newer APK installs over the older one. Between channels it doesn't: the keys differ.

docs.title: An update won't install over the app ("App not installed")
docs.text:
The new APK is signed with another key than the installed one (a release over a preview or a self-built app, or the other way round). Stay on the channel you have, or move like this:

  1. In the app you have: Settings → Backup → Save settings to a file (language, pinned and muted chats, call settings, connected subscription services).
  2. Uninstall it, install the other APK, and pair again (hivepal pair): conversations, agents and calls come back from the relay.
  3. Settings → Backup → Restore from a file. Then put the widget back, log in again to the services in Subscriptions, and remove the old phone from the relay (hivepal devices revoke <id>).

docs.title: Can I use it on iPhone?
docs.text: Not yet: there's only the Android app.

docs.title: Can I keep using agentring?
docs.text: Hivepal's relay speaks agentring's protocol plus its own additions, and reads AGENTRING_* settings. The app has the same package name as agentring's, so you can't have both installed unless you build Hivepal with -PhivepalApplicationId=your.id.

docs.title: Where's my data?
docs.text: On your server, in one SQLite file, and on the phone. What's stored where.

docs.title: Push notifications with your own Firebase project
docs.text:
hivepal wakes your phone with Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) high-priority data messages. You use your own free Firebase project: nothing goes through anyone else's servers, and the prebuilt APK works with it without rebuilding — the relay hands the app the (public) client settings when you pair.

Firebase is optional: without it the app is woken through UnifiedPush, with the free ntfy app (no Google account), and a locked phone rings the same. Choose Firebase if you'd rather not install another app and already use Google services on the phone; with both available, each phone picks one in Settings → Notifications.

Time: ~5 minutes. Cost: free (FCM has no usage charges).

docs.title: 1. Create the project
docs.text:
1. Open https://console.firebase.google.com and click Create a project.
  2. Name it (e.g. hivepal). Google Analytics is not needed — turn it off.

docs.title: 2. Register the Android app
docs.text:
1. In the project overview click the Android icon (Add app → Android).
  2. Android package name: dev.agentring.app — exactly this.
  3. App nickname: anything. Leave the SHA-1 empty.
  4. Click Register app, then Download google-services.json.
  5. Skip the remaining "Add Firebase SDK" steps (the app already contains it).

docs.title: 3. Create a service account key (lets the relay send pushes)
docs.text:
1. Click the gear ⚙ → Project settings → Service accounts tab.
  2. Click Generate new private key → Generate key. A JSON file downloads.
  3. Treat this file like a password: anyone holding it can send pushes to your phone through your project.

The Cloud Messaging tab should show Firebase Cloud Messaging API (V1): Enabled (the default for new projects). If it says disabled, enable it there.

docs.title: 4. Give both files to the relay
docs.text:
On the relay server, with the docker compose deployment:

cd deploy
cp ~/Downloads/google-services.json        secrets/google-services.json
cp ~/Downloads/hivepal-*-firebase-adminsdk-*.json secrets/firebase-service-account.json
chmod 600 secrets/*.json
# The relay runs as uid 1000 inside its container. If your user on the server isn't
# uid 1000 (check with `id -u`), hand the files to that uid so the relay can read them:
sudo chown 1000:1000 secrets/*.json

In deploy/.env uncomment:

FCM_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_FILE=/secrets/firebase-service-account.json
FCM_GOOGLE_SERVICES_FILE=/secrets/google-services.json

Restart: docker compose up -d. The relay log should say "push":"fcm", and hivepal status shows Push: fcm.

Running the relay without docker? Point the same two environment variables at the files.

docs.title: 5. (Re-)pair the phone
docs.text: The app learns the Firebase settings when it pairs. If you paired before configuring Firebase, pair again: in the app Settings → Unpair this phone, then hivepal pair on your computer. The app's Home screen should show Push: Registered, and hivepal status shows push ok for the device.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix Relay keeps restarting with EACCES: permission denied on /secrets/…json The files are chmod 600 and owned by a user other than uid 1000, the relay's user in the container: sudo chown 1000:1000 deploy/secrets/*.json. Relay fails to start: google-services.json has no Android app with package name "dev.agentring.app" You registered a different package name. Add another Android app with dev.agentring.app and download the new file. If you build the app under your own id (-PhivepalApplicationId=…), register that id and set HIVEPAL_ANDROID_PACKAGE to it in deploy/.env. Home shows Push: Unavailable: Google Play services The phone has no Google Play services (e.g. some Huawei / de-Googled ROMs). Use a UnifiedPush distributor such as ntfy in Settings → Notifications. Home shows Push: Error … Check the phone has internet, then reopen the app. Make sure the relay was restarted after adding the files and that you re-paired. hivepal status says NO push token The app never registered: open it once; check the Home screen's Push row. Pushes arrive late or not at all with the screen off Battery optimisation: see troubleshooting-oem.md.

docs.title: Multi-agent fork
docs.text: Hivepal lets several agents share one relay, each with its own identity, instead of one agent per relay (upstream agentring's model).

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
• Agents. The relay's API key is the agent main (the voice daemon on the VPS uses it). Every other agent gets its own ak_ key: hivepal bots add <id> <Name> (relay key only). An agent's key opens only its own conversations and calls; it can't pair phones or manage agents.
  • Conversations. Every message has a conv: agent:<id> (the user and one agent) or group:<id> (the user and several agents). Messages from before the fork are agent:main.
  • Groups. hivepal groups add <id> <Name> --members a,b,c, or from the app. Every member reads what the user and the other members write there (hivepal msg --group <id>, hivepal replies shows [Group] Author: text).
  • Names. The user renames agents from the app (PATCH /v1/agents/{id}); agent.updated and group.updated events keep every phone in step.
  • Calls carry agent_id and the agent's name. User→agent calls still go to main.
  • Presence. One WebSocket per agent (upstream allowed one per relay); agent.presence has agent_id.

Protocol: protocol/relay.openapi.yaml (/v1/agents, /v1/groups, conv on messages). Tests: relay/test/multiagent.test.ts, daemon/tests/test_multiagent.py.

docs.title: Hivepal additions
docs.text:
• Quick replies: an agent sends options (≤ 6, ≤ 40 chars); the app shows buttons under the message (and 2 in the notification); tapping one posts it with reply_to. The CLI shows Sí (reply to: «question»).
  • Attachments: POST /v1/files (raw body, image/jpeg|png|webp, audio/mp4|aac|ogg|mpeg|webm, ≤ 10 MB, stored in SQLite) and attachments: [file_id] on a message. An agent downloads files it uploaded or that are attached to a message it can see.
  • Reminders: POST /v1/reminders {text, at, conv?, options?}; the relay posts the message as the agent at at (checked every 10 s), with a push. Canceled when the agent or its group is gone.
  • Bot conversations: bots:<a>.<b> (ids sorted). Both agents read and write; the user reads it in the app ("Between agents"); it never pushes.
  • Calling an agent: the phone sends agent_id in POST /v1/calls; the voice daemon (main) answers every user call and speaks as that agent, with personas/<agent_id>.md from its home (for example synced from wherever you keep each agent's notes).
  • Last seen: last_seen_at on /v1/agents, updated (once a minute at most) on every request with the agent's key; the app shows it and turns it red after a day.
  • Pairing link: PairingToken.qr_url = <relay>/pair#<base64url of qr_payload>. GET /pair is a static page (CSP by script hash; the code stays in the fragment) that offers to install the app and opens it with hivepal://pair?c=<code>; the app shows the relay's host and asks before pairing.
  • Test call: POST /v1/calls/test {delay_s} (phones only): after the delay the relay places a call from main targeted at that phone, through the normal call path ("Ring me in 10 s").
  • UnifiedPush: POST /v1/device/unifiedpush {endpoint, p256dh?, auth?} (https on a public host, re-checked after DNS; DELETE goes back to FCM). The relay POSTs the same signed PushData there, encrypted for the app with RFC 8291 when it gave keys; 404/410 forget it. Device.push_via says unifiedpush, fcm or none. Accepted deviation: architecture.
  • Wake-up emails: PUT /v1/agents/{id}/wake {email} (relay key; the address never shows in views, only wakes), and POST /v1/agents/{id}/wake/test, which sends it now and answers 204 or 502 email_failed with what the mail server said.
  • Delivery and memory (issue #41, accepted deviation): the relay's email account (PUT /v1/settings/email, logs in before saving; replaces HIVEPAL_SMTP_URL), mailboxes per agent or for all (PUT /v1/agents/{id}/mailbox, PUT /v1/settings/mailboxes): an inbox/ file per message received, in a git repository per agent in the relay (git clone https://x:<key>@relay/v1/agents/<id>/mailbox.git) and, when set, an external repository (PUT /v1/settings/mailbox-repo, the relay's deploy key in GET /v1/settings/delivery), pushed after a short batch and then the wake-up email. Memory (PUT /v1/settings/memory {markdown, sqlite}): history/<conversation>/<day>.md in the mailbox, and/or GET /v1/agents/{id}/memory?q= (FTS5) and /memory.sqlite. Phones may change all of it (the app); an agent reads only its own.
  • Typing (issue #48): POST /v1/typing {conv?, typing?} (agents) shows "typing…" on the phones for 20 s; the relay also sets it for 60 s when an agent marks a message the user sent in the last 10 minutes as read (what hivepal replies does), and ends it when the agent writes there. It's an ephemeral agent.typing event, like agent.presence: never stored, never pushed.
  • What a relay is configured for: Status.features {calls, voice, wake_email}, to agents (used by hivepal doctor and the web panel).
  • Web panel: GET /admin, a static page that uses the REST API with the relay's key pasted into it (kept in that tab): status, phones and a pairing QR, agents with setup to copy, a test message and a test call.

docs.title: App
docs.text:
Navigation drawer (Chats, Calls, Agents, Reminders, Subscriptions, Status, Settings). One chat per agent and per group, with a colour per agent; a chat's menu clears it on this phone (the relay keeps the messages), renames the agent or edits the group. Calls lists the call history with missed calls marked; Settings can copy agent calls into the Phone app's call log (WRITE_CALL_LOG, optional), choose how the phone is woken (Firebase or UnifiedPush), check for updates, save and restore the app's settings to a file, and ring the phone as a test.

The app keeps the package dev.agentring.app, so it can't be installed over the Play Store build (different signing key): uninstall that first and pair again.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: An upstream daemon works with the fork: with the relay key it is main; with an agent's own key it gets that agent's conversation (but can't write in groups). The fork's app works with an upstream relay too: then there is only main.

docs.title: Protocol (v1)
docs.text: Status: proposal for M1 review. The normative definition is protocol/relay.openapi.yaml; this document explains the flows.

docs.title: Principals and authentication
docs.text:
Principal Credential Header agent (the daemon) API key ak_… (random 32 bytes, base64url) Authorization: Bearer ak_… device (the phone) device_jwt (HS256, iss=relay_id, sub=device_id, aud=device) Authorization: Bearer eyJ… LiveKit server LiveKit webhook signature Authorization: <livekit jwt>

In hub mode the agent may also use a short-lived agent token at_… issued by the hub admin API (cloud.md); it works like the API key until it expires.

The relay tells credentials apart by prefix (ak_, at_) vs JWT shape. TLS is mandatory in production; the relay refuses to start with a non-https public URL unless HIVEPAL_INSECURE_DEV=1.

Every device request re-checks the device row, so DELETE /v1/devices/{id} revokes immediately (REST returns 401, open WebSockets are closed with code 4401). A phone on the open call also ends that call: its room closes, which is what takes back a join token LiveKit keeps refreshing.

docs.title: Identifiers and time
docs.text:
• IDs are prefixed ULIDs (lexicographically sortable): dev_…, call_…, msg_…, evt_…. The relay itself has a relay_id (rly_…) generated on first start.
  • All timestamps are integer milliseconds since the Unix epoch (UTC).

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Every event is a flat JSON object:

{ "type": "msg.new", "id": "evt_01JB…", "ts": 1761200000000, "seq": 42,
  "msg_id": "msg_01JB…", "from": "agent", "text": "Build finished ✅" }
Field Meaning type discriminator (below) id unique event id; clients de-duplicate on it (an event can arrive by FCM and WS) ts creation time, ms seq position in the relay's event log (monotonic, global, may have gaps per principal). Absent on ephemeral events.

docs.title: Catalogue
docs.text:
type Payload Persisted Emitted when call.invite call_id, direction, agent_name, reason, priority, expires_at, device_ids? ✓ a call is created; addressed to the callee side (device_ids only on a targeted call) call.ringing call_id, device_id ✓ a device shows the incoming call UI call.accept call_id, by, device_id? ✓ a callee answered (in a group call, once per phone that joins, by accept or join) call.decline call_id, by, device_id? ✓ a callee declined (in a group call, only that phone) call.end call_id, by, reason, duration_ms? ✓ either side hung up, caller canceled while ringing, or LiveKit closed the room call.missed call_id ✓ no answer after RING_TIMEOUT_S (default 30) msg.new msg_id, from, text, reply_to?, truncated? ✓ a message was posted msg.read msg_id, by ✓ the other side read it agent.presence online ✗ daemon WS connected / disconnected (devices only) ws.hello relay_id, last_seq, server_ts ✗ first frame on every WebSocket agent.typing agent_id, conv, typing, until? ✗ Hivepal: an agent started or stopped writing (devices only; a phone that connects gets who is writing now)
  • direction: agent_to_user (agent calls phone) or user_to_agent.
  • priority: normal | urgent. Urgent = alarm stream + bypass DnD if the user granted policy access.
  • by: agent | user | relay (relay = timeout / room closed).
  • call.end.reason: hangup | canceled | room_closed | error.
  • expires_at on call.invite: the app must not ring after this time (late FCM delivery).
  • msg.new.truncated is only ever true inside a push payload (FCM data is capped at 4 KB); the app then fetches GET /v1/messages/{msg_id}.

docs.title: REST (commands)
docs.text:
All mutations are REST calls (see OpenAPI). Errors have the shape {"error": {"code": "busy", "message": "…"}}.

POST /v1/messages accepts an optional client_msg_id; retries with the same value return the original message (idempotency for flaky mobile networks).

docs.title: WebSocket (event stream)
docs.text:
GET /v1/ws?after_seq=<n> with the usual Authorization header.

  1. Server sends ws.hello.
  2. Server replays every persisted event visible to the principal with seq > after_seq, then streams live events.
  3. Client → server frames are not used in v1 (keepalive via WS ping/pong every 20 s; the relay drops sockets silent for 60 s).

GET /v1/events?after_seq=<n> returns the same thing as a page, for clients that only want to catch up (e.g. hivepal replies when serve isn't running).

Visibility: both principals see all persisted events; each side acts on them according to direction/from. Devices additionally get agent.presence. The exception is a targeted call (see Targeted calls): its call.* events reach only the agent and the phones it targets, on the WebSocket (live and replay), over FCM and in GET /v1/events. Because of that a page of GET /v1/events can hold fewer events than limit; page on its next_after_seq.

docs.title: Push (FCM)
docs.text:
Sent through the PushProvider interface:

interface PushProvider {
  readonly name: string;                       // "fcm" | "unifiedpush" (future)
  send(target: PushTarget, payload: PushPayload, opts: PushOptions): Promise<PushResult>;
}
interface PushOptions { ttlSeconds: number; highPriority: boolean; collapseKey?: string }
type PushResult = { ok: true } | { ok: false; unregistered: boolean; error: string };

FCM HTTP v1 message (data-only, never a notification block, so the app always handles it itself):

{
  "message": {
    "token": "<fcm_token>",
    "android": { "priority": "HIGH", "ttl": "30s" },
    "data": {
      "v": "1",
      "relay_id": "rly_01JB…",
      "event": "{\"type\":\"call.invite\",…}",
      "sig": "<base64url HMAC-SHA256(push_secret, event)>"
    }
  }
}

Which events are pushed to devices:

Event TTL Why call.invite (agent_to_user) until expires_at (≤ 30 s) ring call.end / call.missed of an agent call 30 s stop ringing / tear down the call screen on all devices call.accept of an agent call (normal priority), to every phone except the one that joined 1 h offer "join the call" on the phones that are not on it

A targeted call's pushes go only to the phones it targets. | msg.new (from: agent) | 28 days | notification |

call.accept goes at normal priority: a phone still ringing has nothing to show for it, and high-priority pushes that show nothing get an app's later pushes deprioritized by FCM; a phone in Doze gets it at its next maintenance window or when the screen turns on, which is soon enough to offer "join". The TTL is long so a phone that was offline during the ring still learns about the call; the app checks the call (GET /v1/calls/{call_id}) before offering anything. call.decline is not pushed: one phone declining changes nothing for the others.

An UNREGISTERED FCM response clears the device's token (the app will re-send it via POST /v1/device/fcm on next start/refresh).

docs.title: Pairing
docs.text:
hivepal pair
  └─ POST /v1/pairing-tokens  (agent)        → { pairing_token, expires_at, qr_payload }
     prints QR(qr_payload)                      qr_payload = {"v":1,"relay_url":"https://…","pairing_token":"pt_…"}
app scans QR
  └─ POST /v1/pair { pairing_token, fcm_token, device_name, platform, app_version }
       → { device_id, device_jwt, push_secret, relay_id, agent_name, push_config }
     push_config = the user's Firebase client values (or null): the app initialises
     Firebase at runtime, so one prebuilt APK works with anyone's Firebase project
     relay: token single-use (stored hashed), expires after 10 min
app stores device_jwt + push_secret (SecretStore: AES-GCM with an Android Keystore key)
FirebaseMessagingService.onNewToken → POST /v1/device/fcm { fcm_token }

hivepal pair polls GET /v1/devices (or listens on WS) and prints "Paired with Pixel 8 ✅".

docs.title: Message agent → user (M1)
docs.text:
hivepal msg "hola" → POST /v1/messages {text}  (agent) → 201 {msg_id}
relay: store, event msg.new(from=agent) → WS (all) + FCM (devices)
app: verify sig → notification (MessagingStyle, inline reply)

docs.title: Reply user → agent (M1)
docs.text:
app (inline reply or thread) → POST /v1/messages {text, client_msg_id, reply_to?}  (device)
relay: event msg.new(from=user) → WS
daemon serve: store locally          hivepal replies [--since]
(daemon not running: `hivepal replies` falls back to GET /v1/messages?from=user)

docs.title: Outbound call (agent → user) (M2)
docs.text:
daemon: POST /v1/calls {reason, priority}  (agent)
  → 201 { call: {state: ringing,…}, join: {livekit_url, livekit_token, room} }
  daemon worker joins the room immediately
relay: create LiveKit room "call_<id>", event call.invite → WS + FCM, start 30 s timer
app: FCM → verify → ConnectionService.addNewIncomingCall → CallStyle + FSI
     → POST /v1/calls/{id}/ringing
user answers → POST /v1/calls/{id}/accept → 200 { call, join }  → app joins room
relay: state active, event call.accept
hang up (either side) → POST /v1/calls/{id}/end → state ended, event call.end
no answer in 30 s → state missed, event call.missed → daemon sends msg.new(reason) fallback (M4)

docs.title: Inbound call (user → agent) (M4)
docs.text:
app: POST /v1/calls {reason?}  (device)  → 201 { call, join }  → app joins & waits
  (503 agent_offline if no daemon WebSocket is connected)
relay: event call.invite(direction=user_to_agent) → WS
daemon: POST /v1/calls/{id}/accept → join → starts worker

App side ("Call agent" button, enabled while the relay WebSocket is connected and the agent is online):

  • The phone joins the LiveKit room right away with the join from the 201 and shows "Calling …". It switches to the in-call screen on the first of: call.accept on the WebSocket, the agent participant joining the room, or GET /v1/calls/{id} returning active (polled every 2 s, because events of calls to the agent are not pushed by FCM and the socket may be down).
  • Hanging up while it rings → POST /v1/calls/{id}/end (relay: canceled).
  • call.decline / state declined → "The agent declined the call"; call.missed / state missed → "The agent didn't answer"; the call screen shows the message briefly and closes. As a last resort the app gives up after 75 s (ends the call itself).
  • 503 agent_offline, 503 calls_unavailable and 409 busy are shown under the button; no call screen opens.
  • The phone ignores the call.invite of its own call (direction: user_to_agent never rings a phone).

docs.title: Call states
docs.text:
accept                 end
ringing ───────────▶ active ───────────▶ ended
   │ decline ─▶ declined
   │ timeout ─▶ missed
   └ caller end ─▶ canceled

LiveKit room_finished webhook on an active call → ended with by: relay, reason: room_closed (covers crashes and lost connectivity).

docs.title: Group calls (agent → user)
docs.text:
Every paired phone rings. Each may answer while the call rings (until expires_at); they all join the same room and hear the agent and each other. A phone declining or hanging up only affects itself. The call ends when the agent hangs up, or when the last phone leaves (once nobody else can still answer, i.e. after the ring window or when no phone is still ringing). It is declined only if every phone declined, missed if nobody answered.

Join the call. While the call is active, any paired phone that is not on it (its ring ended, it declined, it hung up, or it never got the invite) may join at any time with POST /v1/calls/{call_id}/join → { call, join } (same JoinInfo as accept). While the call still rings, join is the same as accept, so a client can always use it for "join". It emits call.accept with the phone's device_id; a phone already on the call just gets a new token. 409 call_ended once the call is ended/missed/declined/canceled. An empty call still ends (rule above), so "join" is only offered while someone is on it.

How a phone learns it can join: the call.accept push (or WebSocket event) of another phone, the response of its own decline / end (state still active), its own ring timing out locally (it checks GET /v1/calls/{call_id}), and active_call in GET /v1/status when the app comes to the foreground. It stops offering it on call.end / call.missed or a 409 call_ended.

docs.title: Targeted calls (agent → some phones)
docs.text:
The agent may ring only some phones, e.g. calling back just the person who asked ("call me when it's done") instead of waking everyone:

POST /v1/calls {"reason": "The report is ready", "device_ids": ["dev_…"]}

device_ids (agent only) lists paired, non-revoked phones (GET /v1/devices); duplicates are ignored. Unknown or revoked ids, an empty list, or a phone sending device_ids → 400 invalid_request. Without it, every paired phone rings (group call, above).

A targeted call is private to its phones. Only they get participant rows, the call.invite (WebSocket and push) and every later event of the call, and only they can answer, decline or join it; the group-call rules above apply among them. Every other phone gets no event or push for it, so it never rings or offers "join", even with an old app: the filtering is done by the relay. For those phones the call does not exist: GET /v1/calls/{call_id} is 404, it is left out of GET /v1/calls and of active_call in GET /v1/status, end is 404 too, and accept / decline / join are 403 forbidden (ringing is ignored). It still blocks new calls while it rings or is active (409 busy, one call at a time). The Call object and the call.invite event carry device_ids.

A LiveKit participant_left for a phone's older session (e.g. kicked by its own rejoin with the same identity) does not take it off the call: the relay compares the session's join time with the phone's latest join.

docs.title: LiveKit
docs.text:
• Room call_<call_id>, emptyTimeout 30 s, created by the relay.
  • Identities: agent, device_<device_id>.
  • Token: one room, canPublish, canSubscribe, canPublishData, TTL 120 s (join window only; an established session is not affected).
  • Live transcript: not implemented yet. The daemon keeps the transcript of AI calls (hivepal call --ai --json, the MCP call tool); the app does not show it.

docs.title: Hosted relays (hub mode)
docs.text: A hosted relay (docs/cloud.md) serves each tenant under a base URL with a path, https://host/t/{tenant_id}; clients append /v1/... to it as usual. It may refuse POST /v1/pair, /v1/calls and /v1/messages with 402 quota_exceeded when the plan's limit is reached, end an active call with end_reason: "quota" when the call minutes run out (until then GET /v1/calls/{call_id} shows time_left_ms, so a voice agent can warn the user), and answer 403 tenant_disabled for a disabled account. A self-hosted relay never does any of this.

docs.title: Daemon local HTTP API (M5, sketch)
docs.text:
Bound to 127.0.0.1:7878 by default, Authorization: Bearer <local key>.

Method Path Body / query Response POST /call {reason, priority?, wait?} {call_id, status, summary?} POST /message {text} {msg_id} GET /replies ?since=<ms or msg_id> {messages: [...]} GET /calls/{id} {call_id, status, duration_ms?, summary?, transcript?}

The MCP streamable-HTTP transport is mounted on the same server at /mcp.

docs.title: Releasing hivepal
docs.text:
Pushing a tag vX.Y.Z runs .github/workflows/release.yml. It builds everything first and publishes only once every build has succeeded:

Artifact Where it goes Android APK signed with the release key (hivepal-X.Y.Z.apk) GitHub release Daemon sdist + wheel (hivepal on PyPI) PyPI (trusted publishing) and the GitHub release ghcr.io/<owner>/hivepal-relay:X.Y.Z and hivepal-daemon:X.Y.Z (amd64 + arm64, SBOM + provenance) GitHub Container Registry; latest too for final releases SHA256SUMS of every file in the release GitHub release

Pre-releases use PEP 440 suffixes: v0.3.0a1, v0.3.0b2, v0.3.0rc1. They are marked as pre-releases on GitHub, don't move the latest image tag, and pip only installs them when asked for explicitly. Other tag shapes (v0.3, v0.3.0-rc.1) are rejected.

The Android versionCode is derived from the tag so that every release upgrades the previous one: major·1000000 + minor·10000 + patch·100 + slot, where the slot is N for aN, 30+N for bN, 60+N for rcN and 99 for the final release (v0.2.0rc1 → 20061, v0.2.0 → 20099).

docs.title: When to release, and the two Android channels
docs.text:
There is no schedule: release when main has something worth installing, and say what in CHANGELOG.md. Every pull request that changes behaviour adds a line under Unreleased; that section is what the next release ships. A patch (0.4.1) only fixes things, a minor (0.5.0) adds features (before 1.0 it may also change the protocol, which the changelog must then say).

Channel Built from Signed with Version Release (hivepal-X.Y.Z.apk) a vX.Y.Z tag the release key from the tag (above) android-preview every push to main the public debug key scripts/app-version.sh: last release + commits since (0.4.0+2.ga6e21e1), versionCode 100000000 + commits

scripts/build-app.sh numbers its builds like android-preview. Within a channel every newer build installs over the older one. Across channels it doesn't (different keys): moving a phone from one channel to the other means uninstalling, and pairing it again.

docs.title: 1. Release signing key
docs.text:
The key that signs the APK can never change: Android refuses to update an app signed with a different key, so losing it means every user has to uninstall and reinstall. Generate it once, on your own machine, and keep an offline backup of the file and its password (e.g. in a password manager).

keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore hivepal-release.jks -storetype PKCS12 \
  -alias hivepal -keyalg RSA -keysize 4096 -validity 10000 -dname "CN=hivepal"

keytool ships with any JDK ($JAVA_HOME/bin/keytool). It asks for a password; a PKCS12 keystore uses the same one for the key.

Note the certificate's SHA-256 fingerprint (lowercase, no colons, the way apksigner prints it) for the optional check in step 2:

keytool -list -v -keystore hivepal-release.jks -alias hivepal \
  | sed -n 's/.*SHA256: //p' | tr -d ':' | tr 'A-F' 'a-f'

APKs signed with this key don't install over the debug-signed builds of the android-preview pre-release (same package name, different key). Testers coming from those need to uninstall first.

docs.title: 2. GitHub secrets and variables
docs.text:
Repository → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions:

Name Kind Value HIVEPAL_KEYSTORE_BASE64 secret the keystore, base64 on one line HIVEPAL_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD secret keystore password HIVEPAL_KEY_ALIAS secret hivepal (the -alias above) HIVEPAL_KEY_PASSWORD secret key password; optional for PKCS12 (defaults to the keystore password) HIVEPAL_RELEASE_CERT_SHA256 variable (optional) the fingerprint from step 1; when set, an APK signed by anything else fails the release

With the GitHub CLI:

base64 < hivepal-release.jks | tr -d '\n' | gh secret set HIVEPAL_KEYSTORE_BASE64
gh secret set HIVEPAL_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD      # prompts for the value
gh secret set HIVEPAL_KEY_ALIAS --body hivepal
gh secret set HIVEPAL_KEY_PASSWORD
gh variable set HIVEPAL_RELEASE_CERT_SHA256 --body <fingerprint>

The workflow decodes the keystore into the runner's temporary directory, sets HIVEPAL_REQUIRE_RELEASE_KEY=1 (so a missing key fails the build instead of falling back to the debug key), deletes the file right after the build and checks that the APK is not signed with the debug certificate.

docs.title: 3. PyPI trusted publishing
docs.text:
No PyPI token is stored anywhere: PyPI trusts this repository's workflow through OpenID Connect.

The pypi job only runs when the repository variable HIVEPAL_PUBLISH_PYPI is true (gh variable set HIVEPAL_PUBLISH_PYPI --body true). Until then a release skips PyPI, attaches the wheel to the GitHub release and its notes say how to install from it.

  1. On pypi.org → your account → Publishing → Add a new pending publisher (the project doesn't exist yet; once it does, use the project's own Publishing page):
  2. PyPI project name: hivepal
  3. Owner: mixx86, repository: hivepal
  4. Workflow name: release.yml
  5. Environment name: pypi
  6. On GitHub → Settings → Environments → New environment pypi. Recommended: Required reviewers (yourself), so every upload waits for a click, and Deployment branches and tags → selected tags → v*.

PyPI versions are immutable: a version that was uploaded can never be uploaded again, even after deleting it. A broken release is fixed with a new version.

Publishing to PyPI makes the daemon's source (the sdist) public even while this repository is private.

docs.title: 4. GitHub Container Registry
docs.text:
Nothing to create: the images job pushes with the workflow's own GITHUB_TOKEN (packages: write is granted to that job only). The first push creates the packages hivepal-relay and hivepal-daemon under the owner's account, linked to this repository through the org.opencontainers.image.source label.

New packages of a private repository are private. To let anyone pull them: the package's page → Package settings → Change visibility → Public.

If the organisation or repository restricts workflow permissions (Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions), it must still allow jobs to request packages: write, contents: write and id-token: write.

docs.title: 5. Protect main and the release tags
docs.text:
Hivepal's repository has two rulesets (Settings → Rules → Rulesets):

  • main: changes land only through a pull request, squash-merged, once the required checks pass (Relay + daemon tests, docker compose smoke test (…), Build APK + emulator end-to-end); no force pushes, no deletion, linear history. No one bypasses it. Pull requests need no approval, so the maintainer (or an agent working for them) can merge their own, and auto-merge (gh pr merge --squash --auto) merges one by itself when CI turns green.
  • release tags: only repository admins may create, move or delete v* tags. Anyone who can push a v* tag can publish a release.

The repository also merges by squash only and deletes a branch once its pull request is merged.

docs.title: Cutting a release
docs.text:
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
scripts/release.sh 0.4.1        # --dry-run to only prepare the branch locally

scripts/release.sh checks that main is clean and up to date and that CHANGELOG.md has entries under Unreleased. On a branch release/v0.4.1 it writes the version everywhere it is kept (daemon/pyproject.toml + uv.lock, relay/package.json + package-lock.json, the relay's VERSION in relay/src/routes/system.ts, which /v1/status reports) and turns Unreleased into [0.4.1] - <date>. It opens a pull request that merges itself when CI is green, then tags the merged commit v0.4.1 and pushes the tag. The release workflow refuses a tag whose version doesn't match those files or has no changelog section, and puts that section at the top of the GitHub release's notes.

Then follow the run in the Actions tab (approve the pypi environment when asked, if PyPI is on). Between releases main keeps the last release's version; preview builds show how far past it they are (0.4.0+2.ga6e21e1).

If the run fails before the pypi job, fix the problem in a pull request, delete the tag (git push --delete origin v0.4.1 && git tag -d v0.4.1) and tag the fixed main again (git tag -a v0.4.1 -m "hivepal 0.4.1" && git push origin v0.4.1). After PyPI has the version, release a new patch version instead.

docs.title: Building a release APK locally
docs.text:
cd app-android
export HIVEPAL_KEYSTORE_FILE=/path/to/hivepal-release.jks
export HIVEPAL_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD=… HIVEPAL_KEY_ALIAS=hivepal
./gradlew :app:assembleRelease -PversionName=0.4.1 -PversionCode=40199

The same names also work as Gradle properties (-PHIVEPAL_KEYSTORE_FILE=…). Without HIVEPAL_KEYSTORE_FILE, assembleRelease still works but signs with the public debug key and prints a warning: fine for testing, never publish that APK. Without -PversionName/-PversionCode the build is 0.2.0-dev / 1; scripts/build-app.sh passes the preview numbering instead.

docs.title: Google Play
docs.text:
Upstream agentring publishes its app on Google Play under dev.agentring.app. Hivepal doesn't: to publish your own build, use your own application id (-PhivepalApplicationId=) and your own listing. The notes below are upstream's, kept as a reference.

Play takes an Android App Bundle (AAB), not an APK. Build it with the release key, which then acts as Play's upload key (enrol in Play App Signing when creating the app):

cd app-android
export HIVEPAL_KEYSTORE_FILE=/path/to/hivepal-release.jks
export HIVEPAL_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD=… HIVEPAL_KEY_ALIAS=… HIVEPAL_KEY_PASSWORD=…
HIVEPAL_REQUIRE_RELEASE_KEY=1 ./gradlew :app:bundleRelease -PversionName=0.3.0 -PversionCode=30099
# -> app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab

versionCode must grow with every upload. The app targets API 36, which Play requires for new apps and updates from 2026-08-31.

Android Auto stays out of production bundles. Google Play takes calling apps for cars only on its internal and closed testing tracks and rejects a production or open-testing release that contains one, so bundleRelease leaves the car entry point out by default. For a closed-testing track with Android Auto, build a separate bundle with -PhivepalAndroidAuto=true and a higher versionCode, and never promote it to production (android-auto.md). The GitHub APK always includes it.

Play Console items this app needs:

  • Privacy policy: https://agentring.io/privacy. Account deletion: https://agentring.io/delete-account (accounts exist only on hivepal cloud; they are deleted from the dashboard or by email). Self-hosted users have no account.
  • Full-screen intent (USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT): declare "calling app" — incoming calls show over the lock screen.
  • Foreground service types phoneCall and microphone: declare them with a short video of an incoming call being answered (an agent calls, the phone rings locked, the call runs).
  • REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS: restricted on Play. Justify it as a calling app whose calls must ring in Doze; if review rejects it, a Play build can drop the permission and open Settings.ACTION_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATION_SETTINGS instead.
  • Data safety: microphone audio during calls (sent to the user's relay / voice AI, not stored by the app), messages, device identifiers and the FCM token; data in transit is encrypted (https/wss); the user can delete it (unpair, or delete the cloud account).
  • New personal developer accounts must run a closed test (12+ testers, 14 days) before production; organisation accounts don't.

docs.title: Directories
docs.text:
Upstream's listings (MCP Registry, skills, Glama) point at agentring's hosted service; a Hivepal listing would point at your own relay. Kept as a reference.

Where hivepal is listed, and what to refresh after a release:

  • MCP Registry (registry.modelcontextprotocol.io, feeds GitHub's registry and other directories): server.json lists the hosted server (https://agentring.io/mcp) as io.github.mixx86/hivepal. Set its version to the release, then mcp-publisher validate, mcp-publisher login github and mcp-publisher publish from the repository root. A version can be published once.
  • Grok Build plugin marketplace (xai-org/plugin-marketplace): plugins/hivepal is the plugin (the hosted MCP server and a copy of the skill; a test keeps the copy equal). The catalog entry pins a commit of this repository, so after changing the plugin or the skill, open a PR there that bumps the sha and regenerates the index (its CONTRIBUTING.md has the commands).
  • skills.sh: nothing to publish. It lists skills/hivepal from this repository as people install it (npx skills add mixx86/hivepal).
  • Glama (glama.ai/mcp/servers/mixx86/hivepal): it builds the server from this repository with the settings on its admin page (build step uv sync --project daemon --frozen --no-dev, command uv run --project daemon --no-sync hivepal mcp, Python 3.12, placeholder relay URL and API key) and checks that it starts and lists its tools. Auto-release is on: it rebuilds on every GitHub release.
  • awesome-mcp-servers (punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers, Communication): one line in its README; only needs a PR if the description changes.
  • ClawHub: clawhub skill publish skills/hivepal --slug hivepal --version <x.y.z> after changing the skill.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
At the end of this guide your phone rings when your agent calls it, even locked, and you can call your agent back from the app. It takes about 30 minutes the first time.

There are three pieces:

Piece Where it runs What it does relay + LiveKit a VPS, or your own computer pairing, messages, call state, push; LiveKit carries the call audio daemon / CLI (hivepal) the computer where your agent runs the CLI, the MCP server for your agent, the voice AI; only makes outgoing connections, so NAT is fine Android app your phone rings, native call screen, messages

First choose where the relay runs:

A. A VPS with a domain B. Your own computer Works when the phone is anywhere with internet the phone is on the same Wi-Fi, or anywhere over Tailscale You need a Linux server with Docker (a €4 VPS is plenty) and a DNS name Docker on macOS, Linux or Windows, and the computer switched on Security HTTPS with an automatic certificate plain HTTP, accepted only on private and Tailscale addresses

Already running Caddy, Traefik, nginx or Coolify on your server? Use option A with an existing reverse proxy.

docs.title: 1. Firebase: what wakes the phone (5 minutes, free)
docs.text:
A locked phone, or one where the app is closed, only rings if a push notification wakes it. hivepal uses your own free Firebase project for that: follow firebase.md and you end up with two files. Put both in deploy/secrets/ of your checkout:

deploy/secrets/firebase-service-account.json
deploy/secrets/google-services.json

Without them, messages and calls only reach the phone while the app is open on screen.

docs.title: 2. The relay
docs.text: git clone https://github.com/mixx86/hivepal && cd hivepal/deploy

docs.title: Option A: a VPS with a domain
docs.text:
1. Point a DNS record (e.g. relay.example.com) at the server.
  2. Open these ports, in the server's firewall and in any cloud firewall in front of it (Docker-published ports bypass ufw):
  3. TCP 80 and 443: Caddy and its Let's Encrypt certificate;
  4. UDP 50000–50100 and TCP 7881: call audio (LiveKit).
  5. Configure and start:
cp .env.example .env
nano .env      # HIVEPAL_DOMAIN, HIVEPAL_AGENT_NAME, and uncomment the two FCM_ lines
docker compose up -d --build
docker compose logs relay | grep -A2 "API key"
  1. Check it from your computer: curl https://relay.example.com/healthz prints {"ok":true}.

LIVEKIT_NODE_IP is the server's public IPv4; leave it empty to let LiveKit find it over STUN. The LiveKit secret is generated on first start inside a Docker volume and never goes through .env.

docs.title: Option B: your own computer
docs.text:
1. Find the address the phone will use to reach this computer:
  2. same Wi-Fi: the LAN IP, e.g. ipconfig getifaddr en0 (macOS) or hostname -I (Linux);
  3. away from home too: install Tailscale on the computer and the phone, sign in to the same account on both, and use tailscale ip -4 (a 100.x address).

On a LAN, give the computer a fixed IP (a DHCP reservation in your router), or the phone loses the relay when the IP changes. Tailscale addresses don't change. 2. Configure and start:

cp .env.local.example .env.local
nano .env.local   # HIVEPAL_HOST_IP, HIVEPAL_AGENT_NAME, and uncomment the two FCM_ lines
docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml --env-file .env.local up -d --build
docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml logs relay | grep -A2 "API key"
  1. Check it from the phone's browser: http://<HIVEPAL_HOST_IP>:8080/healthz shows {"ok":true}. If it doesn't load, allow incoming connections for Docker in the computer's firewall.

Everything is published on that one address, not on all interfaces: the relay on 8080, LiveKit on 7880 and 7881, and the call audio on UDP 50000–50100.

docs.title: The API key
docs.text: On first start the relay prints its API key (ak_…) once. You can read it again any time with docker compose exec relay cat /data/api_key (add -f docker-compose.local.yml --env-file .env.local for option B). It is the key to your relay: give it only to the daemon.

docs.title: 3. The daemon and CLI
docs.text:
On the computer where your agent runs (it can be the same one as the relay). You need Python 3.11 or later and uv.

uv tool install './daemon[voice]'        # from the repo checkout; [voice] is needed for calls
hivepal init --relay https://relay.example.com --api-key ak_...   # option B: http://<HIVEPAL_HOST_IP>:8080
hivepal status

Its configuration lives in ~/.agentring/ (config.yaml, and the key in .env, mode 600). The HIVEPAL_RELAY_URL and HIVEPAL_API_KEY environment variables override it. To run the daemon on the VPS instead, next to the relay, see the daemon profile at the top of deploy/docker-compose.yml.

docs.title: 4. The app
docs.text:
1. Install hivepal-X.Y.Z.apk from the latest release (Android asks you to allow installs from your browser once); scanning the QR code from hivepal pair with the phone's camera offers it too. Or build it and install it over USB: ./scripts/build-app.sh --install (JDK 17+ and the Android SDK). The app keeps upstream's package name, so if you have agentring from Google Play, uninstall it first (or build with -PhivepalApplicationId=your.own.id).
  2. Open it and tap Get started. It asks, one by one, for notifications, the microphone, full-screen calls on the lock screen and unrestricted battery use: allow them all.
  3. On your computer, run hivepal pair. Scan the QR code it shows with the app, or copy the pairing code it prints and paste it in the app.
  4. The CLI prints Paired with <your phone> ✓, and hivepal status shows push ok next to it. If it says NO push token, the relay has no Firebase files (step 1).
  5. In the app, Settings → Calls lists what calls need. Fix anything that is not OK.

docs.title: 5. Your first message and call
docs.text:
hivepal msg "hello"                 # the phone gets a notification; reply from it
hivepal replies                     # your reply

hivepal call "test"                 # rings; answer and you hear a greeting, then your own voice echoed
echo GEMINI_API_KEY=... >> ~/.agentring/.env   # free key: https://aistudio.google.com/apikey (or another provider: voice.md)
hivepal call "The backup failed" --ai        # a voice AI tells you why it's calling and talks with you

Now lock the phone, wait a minute and run hivepal call "test" --ai again: it should ring like a normal call. If it doesn't, see troubleshooting-oem.md.

To call your agent from the app ("Call agent"), keep hivepal serve --ai running on the computer.

docs.title: 6. Connect your agent
docs.text:
claude mcp add hivepal -- hivepal mcp   # Claude Code; Codex, opencode, OpenClaw, Hermes: docs/agents.md

Then ask it, for example: "Run the migration; if anything fails, call me." Recipes for other harnesses, and how to let the voice AI ask your agents for help during a call: agents.md.

docs.title: When something doesn't work
docs.text: Symptom Check The app won't accept the relay URL It only accepts http:// for private, LAN and Tailscale addresses; anything else must be https://. Pairing fails Open <relay URL>/healthz in the phone's browser. If it doesn't load, the phone can't reach the relay (Wi-Fi, Tailscale, firewall). Messages arrive only with the app open hivepal status says NO push token: put the Firebase files in deploy/secrets/, uncomment the FCM_ lines, restart, and pair again. The phone doesn't ring when locked Firebase (above), then the battery settings for your phone: troubleshooting-oem.md. The call connects but there is no sound Call audio needs UDP 50000–50100 and TCP 7881 open to the phone. On a VPS, set LIVEKIT_NODE_IP to its public IPv4. hivepal call --ai says it needs a key The provider's key in ~/.agentring/.env: GEMINI_API_KEY by default, or OPENAI_API_KEY / XAI_API_KEY / PHONIC_API_KEY (voice.md).

docs.title: Running the relay without Docker (development)
docs.text:
cd relay && npm ci && npm run build
HIVEPAL_INSECURE_DEV=1 HIVEPAL_PUBLIC_URL=http://192.168.1.20:8080 npm start

This covers messages only. Calls also need a LiveKit server (LIVEKIT_URL, LIVEKIT_API_KEY, LIVEKIT_API_SECRET) running with room.auto_create: false; option B sets that up for you.

The relay reads the client address from X-Forwarded-For, trusting one reverse proxy. Set HIVEPAL_TRUSTED_PROXIES to the number of proxies in front of it, or 0 if clients reach it directly.

docs.title: Behind an existing reverse proxy (with calls)
docs.text:
Use deploy/docker-compose.proxy.yml when the server already runs Caddy, Traefik or nginx on 80/443 (it is also what a Coolify "Docker Compose" app points at).

What it exposes: the relay on 127.0.0.1:8095 and LiveKit signalling on 127.0.0.1:7880 (both reachable only through your proxy), plus LiveKit media on UDP 50000–50100 and TCP 7881 on all interfaces. Open those in any cloud firewall in front of the server (Docker-published ports bypass ufw).

Hardening built in: both containers run as unprivileged users with a read-only root filesystem, no Linux capabilities, no-new-privileges and CPU/memory/pid limits; the relay image is pinned by digest, built without npm install scripts and ships without npm/yarn; no secret is passed as an environment variable.

  1. On the server, as root, with the two Firebase files in a directory:
deploy/prepare-host.sh /path/to/firebase-files   # prints LIVEKIT_API_KEY=lk_…

It creates /opt/hivepal/relay (Firebase files + LiveKit secret, uid 1000) and /opt/hivepal/livekit (config + keys.yaml, uid 65534). The LiveKit secret is generated there and never leaves the server.

  1. Environment for the compose app (none of these is secret): HIVEPAL_DOMAIN, LIVEKIT_NODE_IP (the server's public IPv4), LIVEKIT_API_KEY (from step 1), optionally HIVEPAL_AGENT_NAME.

  2. Proxy routes. Caddy example:

hivepal.example.com {
 header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000"
 header -Server
 # LiveKit's admin API and the relay's webhook are internal only.
 handle /twirp/* {
     respond 404
 }
 handle /v1/livekit/webhook {
     respond 404
 }
 handle /rtc* {
     reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:7880
 }
 handle {
     reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8095
 }
}
  1. The relay generates its API key on first start; read it with docker exec <relay container> cat /data/api_key and give it only to the daemon (hivepal init).

docs.title: Calls don't ring: battery savers and OEM background killers
docs.text:
hivepal wakes the phone with a high-priority FCM data message. The app then starts a foreground call service, registers the call with Android's Telecom stack (with its own fallback if that fails) and shows a CallStyle notification with a full-screen intent. If any of those steps is blocked, the call is late or never rings.

Common causes:

  • Doze and App Standby. With the screen off and the phone still, Android defers network access and jobs. High-priority FCM messages are allowed through, but FCM may deprioritize an app whose high-priority pushes don't show a notification, and a "restricted" standby bucket limits them further.
  • "Restricted" battery usage (Android 9+). The app cannot start its call service from the background, so the push arrives but nothing rings.
  • OEM background killers. Xiaomi, Samsung, Huawei, OnePlus, Oppo/Realme and others add their own task killers on top of Android. They can stop the app entirely, so FCM messages are not delivered until you open it again.
  • No Google Play services (most recent Huawei phones, de-Googled ROMs): FCM doesn't work at all. The Home screen shows Push: Unavailable.

docs.title: What the app already checks
docs.text:
The Ready to take calls checklist appears on the onboarding's last screen, on Home whenever a required item is missing, and always in Settings. Each item has a Fix button that opens the right system screen.

Item Needed for Fix opens Notifications required permission prompt (Android 13+) or the app's notification settings Microphone required permission prompt Full-screen calls on the lock screen required (Android 14+ needs explicit permission) Full-screen intents setting for the app Background activity allowed required (not "Restricted") app info Unrestricted battery use strongly recommended (shown in red) the ignore battery optimisations dialog Ring urgent calls in Do Not Disturb optional (hivepal call --urgent) Do Not Disturb access

These are the standard Android settings. OEM-specific switches (autostart, "never sleeping apps", lock in recents) can't be checked by the app; set them by hand as below. Menu names change between versions; if a path doesn't match, search the Settings app for the setting's name, and see dontkillmyapp.com for your exact model.

Settings → Use Android's call system can be turned off if calls misbehave on a particular phone; the app then rings with its own service and notification.

docs.title: Pixel and stock Android (also Motorola, Nokia, Sony, Fairphone)
docs.text:
Usually only the app's checklist is needed.

  • Settings → Apps → hivepal → App battery usage → Unrestricted.
  • Android 14+: Settings → Apps → Special app access → Full screen intents → hivepal on.
  • If you rarely open the app, Android may put it in a lower standby bucket; the "Unrestricted" setting above prevents most of the effect.

docs.title: Samsung (One UI)
docs.text:
• Settings → Apps → hivepal → Battery → Unrestricted.
  • Settings → Battery (or Device care → Battery) → Background usage limits:
  • add hivepal to Never sleeping apps;
  • make sure it is not in Sleeping apps or Deep sleeping apps;
  • consider turning off Put unused apps to sleep.
  • Settings → Apps → hivepal → Notifications: allow, and check the call channels are not silenced.

docs.title: Xiaomi / Redmi / POCO (MIUI, HyperOS)
docs.text:
• Settings → Apps → Manage apps → hivepal:
  • Autostart on;
  • Battery saver → No restrictions;
  • Other permissions → Show on Lock screen and Display pop-up windows while running in the background allowed (needed for the full-screen call screen when locked);
  • Notifications → allow, including lock-screen notifications.
  • Open recent apps, long-press hivepal and tap the lock icon so cleaning the recents doesn't kill it.
  • Disable any "battery saver" / "ultra battery saver" mode while you need calls.

docs.title: Huawei / Honor (EMUI, Magic UI)
docs.text:
• Without Google Play services FCM doesn't work. Use UnifiedPush (setup offers ntfy automatically when the relay has no Firebase); then apply the battery settings below for reliable calls. Older models with Play services:
  • Settings → Battery → App launch → hivepal → turn off Manage automatically, then enable Auto-launch, Secondary launch and Run in background.
  • Settings → Apps → hivepal → Battery → Power-intensive prompt off (if present) and Keep running after screen off on.
  • Lock the app in recent apps.

docs.title: OnePlus (OxygenOS)
docs.text:
• Settings → Apps → hivepal → Battery usage → Allow background activity (older versions: Settings → Battery → Battery optimisation → hivepal → Don't optimise).
  • Settings → Battery → Advanced settings: turn off Optimise battery use / Sleep standby optimisation / Deep optimisation, whichever exist.
  • Lock the app in recent apps.

docs.title: Oppo / Realme (ColorOS, Realme UI)
docs.text:
• Settings → Apps → App management → hivepal → Battery usage: allow foreground activity, background activity and auto launch.
  • Settings → Battery → More settings: turn off Sleep standby optimisation and any App quick freeze that includes hivepal.
  • Lock the app in recent apps.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
1. Check the app's checklist is all green (Settings tab) and Home shows Push: Registered. hivepal status should show push ok for the device.
  2. Force Doze with the phone on USB (or wireless adb) and the screen off:
adb shell dumpsys battery unplug
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle get deep        # should print IDLE

Optionally also simulate a rarely used app: adb shell am set-standby-bucket dev.agentring.app rare.

  1. Place a test call from the daemon (needs the [voice] extra):
hivepal call "test"

It prints a timeline: ringing on dev_… means the phone showed the call (aim for under 5 s); no answer after 30 s with no ringing line means the phone never displayed it.

  1. Restore normal behaviour:
adb shell dumpsys deviceidle unforce
adb shell dumpsys battery reset
adb shell am set-standby-bucket dev.agentring.app active

Real Doze differs from the forced one, and OEM killers usually act after some time with the screen off, so also try with the phone locked and untouched for 10+ minutes before calling.

If it still doesn't ring, collect logs while you call:

adb logcat -s PushHandler HivepalFCM CallManager CallService TelecomBridge Ringer
  • Nothing from PushHandler → the push never reached the app (FCM, Play services or an OEM killer).
  • HivepalFCM: push deprioritized → FCM downgraded the message from high to normal priority.
  • PushHandler: rejected push → the signature or relay id didn't match; pair the phone again.

Then open a bug report with the phone model, Android version, the checklist state and these logs.

docs.title: agentring (upstream README)
docs.text:
The README of agentring, the project Hivepal is forked from, as it was at the fork. Kept for reference: commands and paths here use the upstream names (agentring, AGENTRING_*); in Hivepal they are hivepal and HIVEPAL_*.

Your AI agent can call you. When it needs a decision, hits a wall or finishes a long job, your phone rings like a real call, even locked and in Doze. A voice AI tells you what's going on, you talk it through, and the agent gets the transcript and carries on. You can also call your agents back from the app and ask them things by voice.

Open source, with no phone numbers, no Twilio and no per-minute telephony fees: calls go over VoIP straight to the app. Use the hosted version at agentring.io, or run everything on your own server.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4d925f22-727f-4d66-8665-c392cc3d1eb3

Sound on. A real run with Claude Code, a Pixel 6 and the voice AI: a migration fails, Claude Code calls the locked phone, you decide, it carries on. The phone is a screen recording with the call audio (the ringtone was added), the terminal is redrawn from Claude Code's output, and only the waits were cut. Silent version: demo.gif.

docs.title: Try it in five minutes
docs.text:
With the hosted version there is no server, Firebase project or voice AI key to set up.

  1. Install the app from Google Play (Android 8 or newer).
  2. Sign in at agentring.io with your email (free plan, no card) and scan the QR code on your dashboard with the app. The phone is paired.
  3. Add the MCP server to your agent. The dashboard shows the command with your key:
claude mcp add --transport http agentring https://agentring.io/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ak_…"

Then ask your agent: "run the migration and call me if anything fails."

The free plan has 1 phone, 10 call minutes a month with the voice AI included, and 100 messages a day. Other agents (Codex, opencode, OpenClaw, Hermes, n8n): docs/agents.md. To run it all yourself instead, see Self-hosting.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Your agent reaches you. It can send you a message, wait for your reply or call you (send_message, get_replies, call). On a call, a voice AI explains why the agent is calling, answers your questions and hands the transcript back.
  • You reach your agents. Tap "Call agent" in the app. The voice AI can ask your own agents for help mid-call. If one is slow, the call goes on and its answer arrives when it's ready, or as a message if you've already hung up.
  • Nothing gets lost. A missed call turns into a message you can answer from the notification.

Things people use it for: "run the migration and call me if anything fails", "ask me before you deploy", "what did CI say?" while driving, a daily call with your assistant about your inbox.

docs.title: Works with your agent
docs.text:
agentring doesn't care which harness you use: anything that speaks MCP can reach you, and anything you can run as a command can be consulted from a call.

Reaches you You consult it from a call Claude Code MCP claude -p Codex MCP codex exec opencode MCP opencode run Grok Build MCP, or the plugin OpenClaw MCP openclaw agent Hermes MCP hermes -z n8n, scripts, anything with HTTP REST API, CLI any command, or a small script for an HTTP agent

Copy-paste setup for each: docs/agents.md. OpenClaw and Hermes have one command for all of it: agentring connect openclaw / agentring connect hermes, or install the skill and ask your agent to set agentring up.

The skill installs in any harness that reads skills with npx skills add mutonby/agentring (skills.sh), and from ClawHub as @mutonby/agentring.

docs.title: Self-hosting
docs.text:
Everything on your own machines, free and without limits. You need: - somewhere to run the relay: a Linux server with Docker and a domain name, or your own computer with Docker (the phone on the same Wi-Fi, or anywhere over Tailscale), - a free Firebase project, which is what makes a locked phone ring (docs/firebase.md), - a key for the voice AI: Gemini (free tier), or OpenAI, xAI (Grok), Phonic or OpenRouter (providers), - an Android phone.

# 1. The relay, on a server with a domain (ports 80, 443, UDP 50000-50100 and TCP 7881 open)
cd deploy && cp .env.example .env && $EDITOR .env && docker compose up -d --build
#    ... or on your own computer, at its LAN or Tailscale IP
cd deploy && cp .env.local.example .env.local && $EDITOR .env.local \
  && docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml --env-file .env.local up -d --build
docker compose logs relay | grep -A2 "API key"   # add the same -f/--env-file for the local one

# 2. The computer where your agent runs
uv tool install './daemon[voice]'
agentring init --relay https://relay.example.com --api-key ak_...
agentring pair                         # scan the QR code with the app
agentring msg "hello"                  # the phone gets a notification
echo GEMINI_API_KEY=... >> ~/.agentring/.env  # or OPENAI_API_KEY / XAI_API_KEY / PHONIC_API_KEY
agentring call "Testing agentring" --ai       # + --provider openai|grok|phonic

# 3. Your agent (Claude Code here; others: docs/agents.md)
claude mcp add agentring -- agentring mcp

Install the app from Google Play (recommended: it updates itself, and the same app works with agentring cloud and with your own relay). The APK on Releases is for those who'd rather not use Play; it's signed with a different key, so uninstall one before installing the other. The full tutorial, step by step for both options and with a troubleshooting table: docs/setup.md. If the phone doesn't ring when locked, it's usually the vendor's battery saver: docs/troubleshooting-oem.md.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
your agent ──MCP/CLI──▶ daemon ──WSS (outbound only)──▶ relay ──FCM push──▶ Android app
     ▲                     │                      (your server)                   │
     └── agents.yaml ◀── voice AI (realtime) ◀──────── LiveKit (call audio) ───────┘
  • relay (TypeScript): pairing, messages, call state, push, LiveKit tokens. Runs on your server behind Caddy.
  • LiveKit: the call audio, self-hosted in the same compose file.
  • daemon (Python): the agentring CLI, the MCP server and the voice AI. Runs next to your agents, behind NAT is fine.
  • Android app (Kotlin): QR pairing, the native call screen, messages.

The voice AI is the voice, your agent is the brain: a realtime speech model handles the conversation and hands real work to your agents. Pick the one you like:

Voice AI --provider Key Gemini Live (default, free tier) gemini GEMINI_API_KEY OpenAI Realtime openai OPENAI_API_KEY Grok Voice (xAI) grok XAI_API_KEY Phonic phonic PHONIC_API_KEY OpenRouter: speech-to-text, any chat model, text-to-speech, experimental (details) openrouter OPENROUTER_API_KEY Your own server, e.g. HF speech-to-speech + a small model on llama.cpp (experimental) local none

Set AGENTRING_VOICE_PROVIDER in ~/.agentring/.env to use one for every call, from the CLI and from MCP. How they compare (latency, tool use), how to measure them yourself (agentring voice bench), the local setup and how to add another one: docs/voice.md.

More: architecture · protocol · voice AI

docs.title: Privacy and security
docs.text:
Self-hosted, everything runs on your own servers and accounts (for the hosted version, see its privacy policy). Messages and call metadata are stored on your relay. Push notifications go through your own Firebase project; they are signed, not encrypted, so Google's FCM can read pushed text. Call audio goes through your LiveKit server and, with the voice AI, to the provider you chose (Google, OpenAI, xAI or Phonic); on Google's free tier, Google may use that data to improve its products.

Over the phone, the voice AI acts on what it hears, so give it only the tools and agents you'd trust someone holding your phone with. Details and the threat model: SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Android only (no iOS yet). Android Auto is in beta and only in the APK from Releases: Google Play doesn't allow calling apps for cars in production yet (docs/android-auto.md).
  • It's a young project. The app is on Google Play, and we test it most on a Pixel 6 (Android 16); other vendors' battery savers can hold a call back (docs/troubleshooting-oem.md). If it misbehaves on your phone, please open an issue.
  • Self-hosted, one user per relay: no accounts.
  • The voice AI works best with a cloud realtime model (Gemini, OpenAI, Grok or Phonic). A local one runs on your own machine (--provider local), but it's experimental and slower; others plug in through RealtimeBackend.

cd daemon && uv run --extra voice pytest               # daemon (+ e2e against the relay build)
cd app-android && ./gradlew :core:test :app:assembleDebug
